title: Public Citizen Health Research Group v. Tyson (1986)
shortTitle: Public Citizen Health Research Group v. Tyson (1986)
summary: The assigned opening affirms OSHA’s long-term ethylene-oxide limit and remands its omission of a short-term limit for want of record support.

sections.Parties: Public Citizen Health Research Group and other petitioners sought review of an Occupational Safety and Health Administration exposure standard; the named respondent Tyson represented the agency.
sections.Material Facts: OSHA regulated ethylene oxide, used in manufacturing and sterilizing hospital instruments. Its final rule set a long-term exposure limit but omitted a short-term exposure limit. Petitioners challenged both the substantive record support and what they alleged was surrender of the Labor Department’s decisional responsibility to OMB.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit reviewed consolidated challenges to the OSHA rule. The supplied page states the result on the exposure limits, then begins an editorial explanation of the separate presidential-review challenge. The assignment ends before the rest of that discussion.
sections.Issue: Did the record support OSHA’s long-term limit and its omission of a short-term limit? The opening also raises whether OMB pressure displaced authority legally vested in the agency.
sections.Holding: The court affirmed the long-term limit as supported by substantial evidence and remanded the omission of a short-term limit for further consideration because the record did not support it. The supplied page does not disclose the court’s resolution of the separate OMB-displacement argument.
sections.Reasoning: The available passage treats the two exposure decisions separately, preserving the supported portion while remanding the unsupported omission. Its surrounding text asks whether centralized review can operate consistently with the announced principle that OMB does not replace agency authority. Petitioners’ counsel’s account of OMB influence is an argument reported by the editors; the truncated source does not justify converting it into a judicial finding or a holding about executive power.

topics.lrs-o-midnight-rules: The assigned opening follows the transition-rule discussion, but the packet ends before it supplies a complete challenge or holding on withdrawing regulations.
topics.lrs-n-substantial-evidence: The OSH Act requires substantial-evidence review of rules, and the court applied that standard to the long-term limit and the omitted short-term limit.
